source.title: Relating Regularization and Generalization through the Intrinsic Dimension of Activations
source.authors: B. Brown; Jordan Juravsky; Anthony L. Caterini; G. Loaiza-Ganem

page_placements.theme: Representation dimension and geometry change around grokking

record.tranche_reason: The study reproduces the small-transformer modular-division training setup associated with grokking and measures training and validation accuracy over training; it adds activation intrinsic-dimension measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on modular-division grokking. Its image-classification experiments concern regularization and generalization but do not measure delayed generalization, so they are not rows for these claim versions. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: Reproduces the two-layer transformer modular-division (mod 97) grokking setup. It reports training accuracy saturating quickly and validation accuracy jumping from random to 100% much later, across 16 runs sweeping training fraction and weight decay.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a sudden LLID drop co-occurs with grokking, and that activation intrinsic dimension correlates strongly with generalization. The finding that excessive regularization lowers early-layer ID (PID) and harms validation accuracy comes from the CIFAR ResNet experiments, not the grokking ones.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the small-transformer modular-division setup associated with the original grokking work, while adding activation intrinsic-dimension monitoring; the text describes reproducing the training setup but does not provide a direct replication comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data fraction and weight decay affect when grokking occurs and its duration; the text specifically notes later grokking for a lower training-data amount in the p = 0.15, weight decay = 0.01 example.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation LLID drops suddenly at the same time as the validation-accuracy jump. Grokking runs reach an average minimum LLID of 8.53, versus 16.16 for non-grokking runs. At low data fractions an LLID spike precedes the descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking coincides with a sudden drop in the intrinsic dimension of last-layer activations.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be released publicly upon acceptance
record.peer_reviewed: OPT2022: 14th Annual Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning
record.problems: The grokking results are described partly through figures, and the text provides few per-run values. The training-data-size delay is illustrated qualitatively rather than quantified across settings. Sixteen models are reported, with some failing to reach perfect validation accuracy within 40k steps. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: The CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 regularization sweeps and cited results were omitted because they do not measure grokking-like delayed generalization or test the listed versions. No individual plotted trajectories were added where the supplied text gives no readable per-run values.

untested.parts: No quantitative or systematic measurement of how the delay scales with training-set size. Per-run onset steps appear only in Figures 3/7.
No circuit identification or tracking of memorization removal. The only continuous measure, LLID, co-occurs with the jump rather than anticipating it.
The CIFAR experiments have no delayed generalization, and initialization scale is not varied.
Weight decay is varied, but there is no efficiency, critical-dataset-size or ungrokking test.
Adam is used throughout. No optimizer or numerical controls.

missing.what: Per-run grokking onset step and duration across the 16 training-fraction × weight-decay combinations. This is needed to quantify the V1 delay-vs-data-size relation. The text notes only that higher weight decay helps onset.

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope label is dropped. Runs not grokking within the budget, and the qualitative nature of the data-size evidence, are untested or undetermined parts, not scope limits. The Related Work statement that weight decay speeds grokking is cited from Power et al. and is not a row.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports a qualitative example of later grokking at lower training-data fraction, but does not provide a quantitative or systematic estimate of how delay changes across all training-set sizes.

It measures activation intrinsic dimension, but does not identify a generalizing circuit, track memorizing components being removed, or establish that a continuous circuit-progress measure anticipates the accuracy jump.
Image-classification experiments vary regularization but do not test grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data or a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
Weight decay is varied, but the paper does not test whether it favours a more efficient generalizing circuit, predict a critical dataset size, or test ungrokking below such a size.
The study does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations for grokking.
